transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-07
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Maya Solanki (Redwood AE), Jonas Park (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Redwood CSM), Elliot Voss (Arcane CTO), Rina Matsuda (Arcane ML), Marco D'Angelo (Arcane Infra)

Summary:
Quick technical deep dive on supporting extreme sequence lengths (~128k+ tokens), tradeoffs between latency and throughput, KV cache strategies, chunking, attention optimizations and constraints for a VPC / on-prem deployment. Customer is evaluating replacing parts of their in-house runtime for long-document summarization and multi-doc retrieval workflows.

Topics covered:
- KV cache eviction and persistent prefix caching
- Chunking / overlap strategies for 128k+ sequences
- Batching/micro-batching and sequence packing
- Attention optimizations / sparse + flash attention considerations
- Quantization (4-bit, q8, and hybrid) impact on perf and sample quality
- VPC/on-prem networking and cold-start behavior
- Benchmark plan and next steps

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros, then we'll hand off to Jonas for the runtime deep dive.
[00:12] Elliot (Arcane): Hi, Elliot here. We'll mostly listen in; Rina and Marco will get into the weeds.
[00:20] Jonas (Redwood SE): Cool. So high-level goal we understand: Arcane needs consistent latency for long-context summarization — you're targeting end-to-end p95 latency under 8s for 32k requests and want to explore 128k+ as a roadmap. Is that right?
[00:32] Rina (Arcane): Yeah, that's right. Our current pipeline splits docs into ~8k windows and runs a two-pass summarize, but the quality drop is real and the team wants fewer windows so we can maintain global attention signals.
[00:45] Jonas: Understood. We'll talk about two main axes: memory (KV cache management) and compute (attention and batching). We'll also cover quantization and networking.
[01:05] Marco (Arcane Infra): Before you dive in, quick infrastructure note — our staging has racks with 4xA100 per node over 100GbE, but our on-prem has mixed gen cards and a slower interconnect. We're concerned about cold start and large KV syncing across nodes.
[01:22] Jonas: That's the classic problem. There are three patterns we recommend for 128k+ sequences: 1) rolling chunk + streaming recomposition, 2) sparse global tokens with hierarchical attention, and 3) full KV-persistent mode with on-disk prefix cache and intelligent eviction. We'll talk tradeoffs.
[01:45] Rina: Can you expand on "KV-persistent mode"? We tried a naive LRU and end up thrashing.
[01:52] Jonas: Sure. Naive LRU thrashes because the window for reuse is large. Persistent KV mode keeps a prioritized prefix cache: tokens with high retrieval probability or that are reused across sessions are pinned in GPU memory; warm-but-less-frequent kvs go to NVMe-backed fast storage and we stream them in async when needed. You need to tune pin thresholds and the async prefetch window. On-prem network and NVMe throughput are critical.
[02:20] Elliot: So that means less re-encode, but what about latency when a token's KV sits on disk?
[02:28] Jonas: Good question. We benchmarked hybrid setups and saw tail latency spikes if we do synchronous pulls. The trick is to use predictive prefetch and micro-prefetch windows aligned with predicted next-token distributions. Also, when you have stable prefixes (e.g., legal doc headers) pin them.
[02:46] Marco: Our problem is cross-node sharding of KV. If the active KV is split across GPUs we see cross-NIC hops that blow p95. Any guidance?
[02:55] Jonas: Yes, avoid cross-node round trips for hot KV. We recommend co-locating shard leaders for active segments or using a per-request routing policy that pins requests to nodes with required prefix shards. That increases hot-node utilization but keeps network hops low. Redwood's runtime supports affinity routing and automatic fallback when leaders are busy.
[03:15] Rina: About chunking: we currently do fixed-size 8k chunks with 512 overlap. Our summaries still miss long-range dependencies. What's a better approach?
[03:25] Jonas: For 128k you can't do full attention in one pass; you need hierarchical or sliding window with recomposition. Two promising strategies: 1) hierarchical chunking where you compute chunk-level summaries then attend a smaller set of chunk-summary tokens (e.g., compress 8k->256 tokens) with an additional review pass; 2) progressive attention where you keep a sparse global token set (sqrt or top-k tokens per chunk) and run attention to global tokens plus local dense attention. Both reduce compute; hierarchical gives better structure for summarization tasks.
[03:55] Rina: And overlap sizes? 512 seems arbitrary. For docs like legal filings we need more overlap sometimes.
[04:02] Jonas: Overlap tuning is dataset dependent. We typically start with variable overlap proportional to entity density — more overlap around sections with many named entities. Also adaptive overlap: increase overlap if the chunk summary confidence is low.
[04:18] Elliot: Performance numbers — can you give rough latency/throughput tradeoffs for these approaches on 2xA100 and 4xA100?
[04:26] Jonas: Rough ballpark (these are illustrative): full dense attention to 128k is infeasible. Hierarchical: end-to-end p50 on 2xA100 ~1.2s per 8k chunk + 0.9s for global pass; overall end-to-end for 128k schematically around 12-18s depending on number of chunks and overlap. Sparse/global token approach can shave 20-40% off compute if your sparsity heuristic is strong. KV-persistent with prefix caching reduces token encoding cost by up to 60% for repeated prefixes. Quantization (q4_0) can improve throughput 1.6-2x but may slightly increase repetition and reduce fine-grained factuality — needs eval.
[05:05] Marco: Those are within reason. On-prem will be slower. How much does network link quality affect end-to-end?
[05:12] Jonas: A lot. If KV shards require >1 cross-node hop, p95 can multiply. 100GbE is good but you need sub-ms intra-node latency. For VPC hosted deployments we see more predictable network p95. On-prem variability is the main reason to pin critical shards.
[05:27] Priya (Redwood CSM): A quick note: Redwood Console can surface token-level latency and show where KV fetches happened (GPU memory vs NVMe vs remote). That really helps for these investigations.
[05:37] Rina: Great. Now quantization — we've heard q4 and q8 mentioned. We use mixture-of-experts layers which get funky under naive quant. Any tips?
[05:45] Jonas: MoE is tricky — gating decisions can be sensitive to quant noise. We recommend hybrid quantization: keep gating and layer-norm in fp16, quantize feed-forward weights aggressively (q4), and run a small set of calibration prompts to validate gating stability. Also, bias correction helps. Redwood's optimizer has per-layer quant profiles.
[06:05] Rina: Do you support post-training quant only or do you also do quant-aware finetune?
[06:09] Jonas: Both. Post-training quant with per-channel scaling is fast and often okay; quant-aware finetune is best if you can afford retraining to recover gating behavior.
[06:16] Elliot: What's the recommended batch strategy? We have variable-length sequences; packing helps but we fear increased latency for some tail requests.
[06:23] Jonas: Sequence packing is a big win for throughput but it increases head-of-line latency. Two approaches: 1) strict SLO routing (low latency requests go to low-packing lanes), 2) dynamic micro-batching where short requests are batched tightly in high-throughput lanes and long sequences are streamed as low-latency lanes. Redwood lets you configure lane policies per route.
[06:44] Marco: Can you explain streaming recomposition? We currently get the whole chunk result only at the end.
[06:50] Jonas: Streaming recomposition emits partial chunk summaries incrementally, and a background aggregator updates the global summary as chunk results arrive. That reduces perceived latency; you can deliver early drafts to downstream services. It complicates correctness a bit, but for human-in-the-loop summarization it's often acceptable.
[07:05] Rina: Any insights on attention optimizations beyond flash attention? We heard about fused-kernels and block-sparse ops.
[07:13] Jonas: Right — flash attention helps GPU memory usage and throughput. Fused kernels (fused matmul + softmax) reduce kernel launch overhead. Block-sparse attention can help if your sparsity pattern is structured. Another tactic: sequence parallelism where you split sequence dimension across GPUs — great for huge sequences but requires careful KV routing and increases cross-GPU traffic. The runtime picks kernels based on sequence length distribution and hardware; we benchmark to choose the fastest path.
[07:40] Elliot: For private deployments, how does Redwood handle keys and audit logs? Related to our compliance needs.
[07:46] Maya: For private/VPC installs Redwood supports KMS integrations, HSM options for signing, and audit logs can be forwarded to your SIEM. We can red-team the audit export in staging.
[07:55] Marco: Is there an air-gapped install option?
[07:58] Maya: Yes, we have an on-prem air-gapped package; it requires manual sync for model artifacts and we provide an offline installer and deployment checklist.
[08:07] Rina: Back to benchmarks — what's a minimal benchmark we should run to stress 128k behavior?
[08:12] Jonas: Minimal benchmark plan: a) synthetic runner that replays your longest sequences with realistic token distributions, b) an end-to-end pipeline run that includes tokenization, KV warmup, chunk recomposition and any retrieval steps. Measure p50/p95/p99 latency, token/s throughput, NVMe read/write rates, cross-node traffic, and KV miss rates. Start small (single node) then scale. We'll share a runner.
[08:34] Maya: We'll also send a benchmarking workbook with recommended charts for visualizing the KV hotspots.
[08:40] Rina: Are there common gotchas when running these benchs?
[08:44] Jonas: Yes: 1) synthetic token distributions that are too uniform inflate perf; mimic your real token distributions. 2) Cold-start effects — warm the KV by replaying prefixes. 3) Not capturing NVMe latency in bench harness leads to bad surprises.
[08:58] Elliot: What about fallback strategies — if a node gets overloaded mid-run?
[09:02] Jonas: Redwood supports automatic fallback routing to lower-cost model variants (e.g., smaller sequence-window or quantized) and graceful degradation: reduce sparsity thresholds or increase overlap to avoid recomposition failures. Also can queue requests and surface degradation metrics to operations teams.
[09:20] Marco: Any tips on debugging correctness regressions after quantization?
[09:24] Jonas: Run a suite of golden prompts and diff logits and top-k tokens across fp16 and quantized models. Use calibrated prompts that exercise gating (for MoE) and long-range co-reference. Redwood Optimize can track regression alerts on these prompts.
[09:40] Rina: Let's talk cost. How much does 4x throughput improvement via q4 translate into dollars for us?
[09:46] Maya: It depends on your workload and reserved capacity. If you move from fp16 to q4 and keep the same hardware, you may get ~1.6-2x token throughput, so cost per token drops roughly the same, minus engineering and possible eval/regression costs. Redwood Dedicated offers capacity sizing guidance so you can project cost for reserved nodes.
[10:05] Elliot: Okay great. Let's capture specific next steps.
[10:08] Maya: Quick recap: Jonas will run the arch-level 128k benchmark on Redwood staging with Arcane sample workload, Maya will share quant profiles and deployment checklist, Marco will share infra logs. We'll reconvene after the benchmark.
[10:20] Rina: Thanks everyone. A few side notes — we'll likely want a canary rollout plan for on-prem if we move forward.
[10:27] Maya: Yep, canary + automatic fallback is standard. We'll include example rollout config.
[10:35] Elliot: Appreciate the deep dive.
[10:38] Maya: Thanks all.

End of transcript.
